We had some inquiry about reasonable accommodations to attend meetings of this council, boards and commissions of San Rafael. And I wanted to describe that process briefly as it pertains to tonight and any other meetings that we conduct here in San Rafael. Reasonable accommodation under the law for persons with disabilities is mandated by the Americans with Disabilities act, and the city complies with the act, strives to adhere to it in every respect. And our process here at City hall is laid out on the website. If someone believes they require a reasonable accommodation in order to participate, for example, at a City Council meeting, they are to make that request requisite time in advance of the meeting. And then that's referred to our disability coordinator who also serves as our building official, John Jepson. He handles those kind of requests. He also gets involved in dealing with analysis of disability accommodation in construction in San Rafael as well, because he sure knows how to do that. Too. So the process then is that the individual who seeks the accommodation provides information on a form that the city has to describe the request. And then there is a process that then ensues which is iterative in nature as much as necessary in order for the city to understand the nature of the disability claimed and the accommodation that is a desired and reasonable accommodation, as I said, must be provided under the law. I think it's useful when analyzing the adequacy of a city's adherence to the law to look to the courts, which are governed by the same standard. Because a courthouse is a place of public accommodation, just like a city council chamber. And in the courts of California, along with being governed like we are by the ADA, the courts have a rule called Rule 1.100 that requires a reasonable accommodation at the courthouse. And the Judicial Council of California has promulgated rules for all the courts to follow that the courts must adhere to in analyzing request by any person who desires accommodation at the courthouse enabled in order to be able to participate or observe judicial proceedings. So I think it's useful to read what's required there, although they put it in really small print because the judges can read better than I can. But they say, in regard to reasonable accommodation requests at a court for a, all requests for accommodations must include a description of the accommodation sought along with a statement of the impairment that necessitates each accommodation. The court, in its discretion, may require the applicant to provide additional information about the impairment. So that rule that the courts operate under is, I would suggest, the same way that the city's process would be evaluated by a court. We've, of course, never encountered any challenge, and we've successfully been providing accommodation as required and mandated under the law as long as I've been around and, and even before the Americans with Disabilities act long predates my tenure as city attorney. To allocate these funds on an annual basis, the San Rafael City Council submits recommendations for its portion of funds to the countywide Priority Setting Committee, which is made up of city and town council members, a county supervisor and community members representing protected classes under fair housing laws. The Priority Setting Committee then in turn provides recommendations for the three planning areas to the Board of Supervisors and the Board of Supervisors reviews recommendations from the Priority Setting Committee and forwards its recommendations to the US Department of Housing and Urban Development. I just want to note that due to delayed budget approvals at the federal level, the county has not yet received final Notice of the 202425 CDBG Program Allocation amount.
